parsed.title: What Critical Scholars Say About Jesus' Bodily Resurrection - Gary Habermas
parsed.summary: In this chapter, Gary Habermas surveys quotations from critical scholars (John Cook, Dale Allison, Tom Wright, Michael Licona, Robert Gundry) who affirm that Paul and the earliest disciples believed in a bodily resurrection of Jesus, not a ghostly or purely spiritual appearance. Habermas highlights how these admissions from non-conservative scholars are striking and increasingly common, and he uses them to support the historical credibility of the bodily resurrection claim.

atoms.name: Paul believed in bodily resurrection
atoms.statementTechnical: The Apostle Paul taught that the resurrection appearances of Jesus were bodily, consistent with the Gospel accounts (Matthew, Luke, John), not merely spiritual or ghostly.
atoms.statementPlain: Paul believed Jesus rose physically and appeared in a real body, just like the Gospels describe.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Discovery of undisputed Pauline texts that explicitly deny a bodily resurrection or describe the resurrection appearances as purely visionary/spiritual in a way incompatible with bodily existence.
atoms.notes: Habermas cites John Cook's thesis and Dale Allison's agreement that Paul meant bodily resurrection.

atoms.name: Critical scholars increasingly affirm bodily resurrection
atoms.statementTechnical: A growing number of critical (non-conservative) scholars, including Dale Allison, John Cook, Tom Wright, Michael Licona, and Robert Gundry, affirm that the earliest Christian belief was in a bodily resurrection of Jesus.
atoms.statementPlain: Even skeptical scholars now often agree that the first Christians believed Jesus rose bodily.
atoms.falsificationCondition: A comprehensive survey showing that the majority of critical scholars deny a bodily resurrection belief in early Christianity, or that the cited scholars' views are misrepresented.
atoms.notes: Habermas lists multiple scholars and notes this view is 'very widely taught today'.

atoms.name: Dale Allison's personal testimony
atoms.statementTechnical: Dale Allison, though not personally committed to the bodily resurrection side, states that Paul meant bodily resurrection and that he will be in church on Easter.
atoms.statementPlain: Dale Allison says: 'I believe that the disciples saw Jesus and that he saw them and next Easter will find me in church.'
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that Allison's statement is misquoted or that he later retracted it, or that it does not reflect his actual view.
atoms.notes: Habermas reads this quote from Allison's volume three and calls it stunning.

atoms.name: Tom Wright's analogy: resurrection as knowable as Rubicon
atoms.statementTechnical: Tom Wright compared the knowability of Jesus' resurrection to the knowability of Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon.
atoms.statementPlain: Tom Wright said the resurrection is as historically solid as Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon river.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that Wright never made this comparison or that the analogy is misattributed.
atoms.notes: Habermas and the interviewer discuss the quote; Habermas is 'pretty sure it was Wright'.

atoms.name: Robert Gundry's Soma argues against Bultmann
atoms.statementTechnical: Robert Gundry's book 'Soma' defends a bodily resurrection view against Bultmann's influential non-bodily interpretation.
atoms.statementPlain: Robert Gundry wrote a book called 'Soma' (body) to refute Bultmann's view that resurrection was not physical.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that Gundry's book does not actually argue for bodily resurrection or does not engage Bultmann's view.
atoms.notes: Habermas mentions Gundry as one of the first to write on the subject.

atoms.name: Bultmann's view distinguished from Paul's
atoms.statementTechnical: Bultmann may say Paul believed in bodily resurrection, but Bultmann himself does not; one must distinguish between what Paul said and what Bultmann says Paul said.
atoms.statementPlain: Bultmann can acknowledge that Paul believed in a bodily resurrection, but Bultmann personally rejects it.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that Bultmann actually affirmed bodily resurrection or that the distinction is irrelevant.
atoms.notes: Habermas clarifies the difference between Paul's belief and Bultmann's belief about Paul.

atoms.name: Unclassified transcript segments
atoms.notes: Segments that are conversational filler, personal remarks, or not classifiable as claims.
